demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
At 55, Emeka had spent most of his adult life working as a painter, moving from house to house and job site to job site, carrying ladders, drop cloths, and buckets of paint with the easy routine of someone who knew how to make a living by hand. He was married, and until the loss that changed his life, he had seen himself as steady, practical, and not easily shaken. That sense of himself was upended when his wife died unexpectedly. The details remained fixed in his mind in fragments: the sharp interruption of an ordinary day, the sudden rush of emergency response, the sense that everything had become official and irreversible in a matter of minutes. He could still picture the scene in images rather than as a coherent story, as if his mind returned to separate still frames instead of a whole memory. Sometimes those pictures came with no clear visual scene at all, only the full force of grief arriving in his body before he could name where he was or what had set it off. When he tried to speak about her death, he found himself overwhelmed by sorrow that felt immediate and physical, as though he were standing back in the same moment again.

In the weeks and months that followed, Emeka noticed that certain situations struck him with particular force. Ambulances were the most obvious. The sound of one passing his street or pulling up near a job site could freeze him in place, even when he knew it was not for him. At work, the presence of the workplace itself became difficult in a different way. The familiar setting of ladders, extension cords, and unfinished rooms no longer felt neutral. If a client mentioned someone being delayed because of an emergency, or if he saw coworkers gathered around a phone in concern, his attention sharpened immediately. Talk about people losing loved ones was also hard to bear. He would become quiet and withdrawn when neighbors, relatives, or coworkers discussed bereavement, funerals, or the shock of sudden death, and he often found himself wishing he could leave before the conversation went further. What others could discuss as sympathy or shared experience felt to Emeka like being pulled back toward the edge of the same loss.

As time went on, he became increasingly aware of his body's readiness for danger. Even during ordinary days, he felt on guard, as if he had to stay prepared for something happening without warning. At home, a place that should have been restful, he found himself scanning sounds and movements, unable to settle fully. Nighttime was harder than daytime; once it got dark, he felt less safe and more alert, listening for noises in the house and outside, checking himself against every small sound that might mean trouble. He did not describe this as fear in a dramatic sense so much as a constant tension, a bracing of muscles and attention that never quite let him relax. The feeling travelled with him from room to room, and it was especially noticeable when the house was quiet and his wife was asleep nearby. He knew she could see that something had changed, even when he tried to carry on as normal.

Emeka's memories of the traumatic death remained vivid in a particular way. He did not experience them as a complete story he could retell from beginning to end. Instead, he saw pictures: the look of the ambulance, the positions of bodies and objects, the starkness of the moment when he understood what had happened. At other times, the images dropped away entirely and what remained was the emotional intensity - the same wave of grief, shock, and helplessness, arriving without warning and without a clear mental picture to go with it. He was troubled by how quickly it could happen, as if something inside him could be reopened by a sound, a conversation, or a familiar place.

Over time, these experiences changed how Emeka saw himself and his life. He had come to believe that he did not know himself anymore. The man who once worked steadily and moved through the world with confidence felt absent to him, replaced by someone more guarded, more distant, and less able to trust his own reactions. He felt isolated and set apart from others, even among people who cared about him, because he could not easily explain why ordinary reminders had such power or why he remained so watchful. The scale of the loss left him feeling that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, not in a dramatic metaphorical sense, but as a plain description of how different everything now felt from the life he had before.

By the time he sought help, Emeka was tired of living in this state of suspended readiness and recurring grief. He had reached a point where the reminders were harder to avoid, especially at work and at home, and he no longer wanted to keep managing them alone. What brought him in now was the fear that he would remain trapped in this altered version of himself, unable to feel safe at night, unable to tolerate reminders of loss, and unable to recognize the life he once knew. At the same time, he held onto a simple hope that speaking about it might help him understand what had happened to him, and perhaps help him feel like himself again.
